claim: Head movement signals are encoded by the firing rate of vestibular afferents that project to the cerebellum and brainstem.
source: Head movement signals are encoded by the firing rate of vestibular afferents that project to the cerebellum and brainstem.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction without presenting new data, but is supported by citations.

claim: The vestibular nuclei maintain a sensory representation of the head movement for tens of seconds after the vestibular signal ends through a mechanism called velocity storage.
source: The vestibular nuclei maintain a sensory representation of the head movement for tens of seconds after the vestibular signal ends through a mechanism called velocity storage (Fernandez and Goldberg, 1971; Raphan et al., 1979).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Fernandez and Goldberg, 1971; Raphan et al., 1979).

claim: The cerebellum dynamically modulates the activity of the cells that encode velocity storage to control vestibular responses such as compensatory eye movements.
source: The cerebellum dynamically modulates the activity of the cells that encode velocity storage to control vestibular responses such as compensatory eye movements (Yakushin et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Yakushin et al., 2017.

claim: Granule cells receive direct input from vestibular afferents, but cannot maintain the signal long enough to underlie velocity storage, because they produce only transient firing responses.
source: Granule cells receive direct input from vestibular afferents, but cannot maintain the signal long enough to underlie velocity storage, because they produce only transient firing responses.
evidence: This is stated as an inference based on the known properties of granule cells.

claim: UBCs are powerful circuit elements that amplify their input signals by extending them in time and projecting them to numerous granule cells.
source: UBCs are powerful circuit elements that amplify their input signals by extending them in time and projecting them to numerous granule cells (Berthié and Axelrad, 1994; Mugnaini et al., 1994; Mugnaini et al., 2011; Rossi et al., 1995; Nunzi et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: UBCs receive direct input from vestibular afferents and produce long-duration spiking responses.
source: UBCs receive direct input from vestibular afferents, produce long-duration spiking responses, and could therefore contribute to the maintenance of a sensory representation necessary to modulate low-frequency vestibular responses (Rossi et al., 1995; Mugnaini et al., 2011; Balmer and Trussell, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Multiple UBCs connected in series could extend the signal much further than a single UBC.
source: Although a single UBC can prolong its input for seconds, multiple UBCs connected in series could extend the signal much further.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the properties of single UBCs.

claim: There is some evidence suggesting that UBCs provide direct synaptic input to other UBCs.
source: Indeed, there is some evidence suggesting that UBCs provide direct synaptic input to other UBCs (Diño et al., 2000; Nunzi and Mugnaini, 2000; van Dorp and De Zeeuw, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: UBCs may play important roles in diversifying granule cell firing patterns, which is essential for expansion recoding models of cerebellar learning.
source: In addition to prolonging signals, UBCs may play important roles in diversifying granule cell firing patterns, which is essential for expansion recoding models of cerebellar learning (Marr, 1969; Albus, 1971; Ito, 1982; Kennedy et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on cerebellar learning models.

claim: Diversity in UBC responses is due to different subtypes of UBCs that can be classified by their expression of specific proteins or neurotransmitter receptors.
source: This diversity in UBC responses is due to different subtypes of UBCs that can be classified by their expression of specific proteins or neurotransmitter receptors (Nunzi et al., 2002; Nunzi et al., 2003; Kim et al., 2012; Sekerková et al., 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: ON UBCs that express mGluR1 are excited by glutamate.
source: ON UBCs that express mGluR1 are excited by glutamate and OFF UBCs that express calretinin are inhibited by glutamate (Borges-Merjane and Trussell, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: OFF UBCs that express calretinin are inhibited by glutamate.
source: ON UBCs that express mGluR1 are excited by glutamate and OFF UBCs that express calretinin are inhibited by glutamate (Borges-Merjane and Trussell, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: In GRP UBCs, mossy fiber stimulation evoked fast excitatory postsynaptic currents (EPSCs) and a slow inward current that became more prominent with faster stimulation rates.
source: In GRP UBCs, mossy fiber stimulation evoked fast excitatory postsynaptic currents (EPSCs) and a slow inward current that became more prominent with faster stimulation rates.
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 1B.

claim: The latency between presynaptic stimulation and the beginning of the fast EPSC in GRP UBCs was 1.24 ± 0.29 ms.
source: The latency between presynaptic stimulation and the beginning of the fast EPSC was 1.24 ± 0.29 ms (mean ± SD; n = 13)
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological measurements.

claim: The fast EPSCs in GRP UBCs had a low jitter of 0.074 ± 0.046 ms.
source: had a low jitter (defined as the SD of latency; 0.074 ± 0.046 ms; mean ± SD; n = 13)
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological measurements.

claim: The fast EPSCs in GRP UBCs were reliable, having no failures across all cells and trials, which confirms that they were monosynaptic.
source: and was reliable, having no failures across all cells and trials, which confirms that they were monosynaptic.
evidence: This claim is based on electrophysiological data and inference about monosynaptic connections.

claim: The slow EPSCs in GRP UBCs peaked 70.13 ± 33.45 ms after the end of the 200-ms-long 50 Hz stimulus train.
source: The slow EPSCs peaked 70.13 ± 33.45 ms after the end of the 200-ms-long 50 Hz stimulus train
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological measurements.

claim: The decay of slow EPSCs in GRP UBCs was well approximated by an exponential with a time constant of 358.31 ± 213.83 ms.
source: and their decay was well approximated by an exponential with a time constant of 358.31 ± 213.83 ms (mean ± SD; n = 14) (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological measurements and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: In current-clamp recordings, synaptic stimulation produced a burst of action potentials in GRP UBCs that varied in duration from 510 to 900 ms.
source: In current-clamp recordings, synaptic stimulation produced a burst of action potentials in GRP UBCs that varied in duration from 510 to 900 ms (n = 3) (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The synaptic currents in GRP UBCs were confirmed to be mediated by mGluR1 and AMPA receptors because they were blocked by JNJ16259685 and GYKI53655.
source: The synaptic currents in GRP UBCs were confirmed to be mediated by mGluR1 and AMPA receptors because they were blocked by JNJ16259685 and GYKI53655 (99.3 ± 2.4%; paired t-test; p=0.0068; n = 9; mean ± SEM) (Figure 1E and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by pharmacological experiments shown in Figure 1E and F.

claim: GRP UBCs are ON UBCs and their synaptic responses vary from being mediated mainly by mGluR1 to being entirely mediated by AMPA receptors.
source: This indicates that GRP UBCs are ON UBCs and their synaptic responses vary from being mediated mainly by mGluR1 to being entirely mediated by AMPA receptors.
evidence: This is an inference based on the pharmacological data showing variable contributions of mGluR1 and AMPA receptors.

claim: In all P079 UBCs recorded that responded to presynaptic stimulation, a 50 Hz train evoked a slow outward current.
source: In all P079 UBCs recorded that responded to presynaptic stimulation, a 50 Hz train evoked a slow outward current (n = 12).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings.

claim: The slow outward currents in P079 UBCs peaked 52.7 ± 46.86 ms after the end of the 200-ms-long 50 Hz stimulus train.
source: The slow outward currents peaked 52.7 ± 46.86 ms after the end of the 200-ms-long 50 Hz stimulus train
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological measurements.

claim: The decay of slow outward currents in P079 UBCs was well approximated by an exponential with a time constant of 489.2 ± 350.4 ms.
source: and their decay was well approximated by an exponential with a time constant of 489.2 ± 350.4 ms (mean ± SD; n = 11) (Figure 1H).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological measurements shown in Figure 1H.

claim: The outward currents in P079 UBCs hyperpolarized the cells and produced a pause in spontaneous spiking activity that varied from 0.5 to 3.9 s, averaging 1.72 ± 1.19 s.
source: These outward currents hyperpolarized the cells and produced a pause in spontaneous spiking activity that varied from 0.5 to 3.9 s, averaging 1.72 ± 1.19 s (mean ± SD; n = 10) (Figure 1I).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: The outward current in P079 UBCs was mediated by mGluR2 receptors as it was blocked by the mGluR2 antagonist LY341495.
source: The outward current was mediated by mGluR2 receptors as it was blocked by the mGluR2 antagonist LY341495 (96.53 ± 1.79%; paired t-test; p=0.0033; mean ± SEM) (Figure 1J and K).
evidence: This claim is supported by pharmacological experiments shown in Figure 1J and K.

claim: The electrophysiological characteristics confirm that the P079 UBCs that can be visualized in acute brains slices are OFF UBCs.
source: These electrophysiological characteristics confirm that the P079 UBCs that can be visualized in acute brains slices are OFF UBCs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the electrophysiological and pharmacological data.

claim: The slow postsynaptic currents were inward in every GRP UBC and outward in every P079 UBC.
source: The slow postsynaptic currents were inward in every GRP UBC and outward in every P079 UBC (Figure 1L).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 1L.

claim: The capacitance of GRP UBCs was less than half that of P079 UBCs.
source: The capacitance of GRP UBCs was less than half that of P079 UBCs, which suggests that the membrane area of the OFF UBCs is greater (GRP UBCs: 11.34 pF ± 0.59, n = 15; P079 UBCs: 26.08 pF ± 1.96, n = 12; t-test; p<0.0001; mean ± SEM; Figure 1M).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological measurements shown in Figure 1M.

claim: The membrane area of the OFF UBCs is greater than that of ON UBCs.
source: The capacitance of GRP UBCs was less than half that of P079 UBCs, which suggests that the membrane area of the OFF UBCs is greater (GRP UBCs: 11.34 pF ± 0.59, n = 15; P079 UBCs: 26.08 pF ± 1.96, n = 12; t-test; p<0.0001; mean ± SEM; Figure 1M).
evidence: This is an inference based on the capacitance measurements.

claim: There was no significant difference in input resistance between GRP and P079 UBCs.
source: We did not observe a significant difference in input resistance between the two cell types (GRP UBCs: 0.56 GΩ ± 0.04, n = 9; P079 UBCs: 0.64 GΩ ± 0.09, n = 10; t-test; p=0.44; mean ± SEM; Figure 1N).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological measurements shown in Figure 1N.

claim: GRP UBCs had a higher firing rate in response to the same level of injected current compared to P079 UBCs.
source: GRP UBCs had a higher firing rate in response to the same level of injected current compared to P079 UBCs, despite their similar input resistance, suggesting that GRP ON UBCs are more excitable and can fire at faster rates (Figure 1O and P).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 1O and P.

claim: GRP ON UBCs are more excitable and can fire at faster rates than P079 OFF UBCs.
source: GRP UBCs had a higher firing rate in response to the same level of injected current compared to P079 UBCs, despite their similar input resistance, suggesting that GRP ON UBCs are more excitable and can fire at faster rates (Figure 1O and P).
evidence: This is an inference based on the firing rate data.

claim: P079 UBCs had a significantly more prominent sag than GRP UBCs, measured in response to a –100 pA current step.
source: P079 UBCs had a significantly more prominent sag than GRP UBCs, measured in response to a –100 pA current step (P079: 0.39 ± 0.04, n = 7; GRP: 0.16 ± 0.01, n = 15; t-test; p<0.0001; mean ± SEM) (Figure 1P and Q).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological measurements shown in Figure 1P and Q.

claim: The larger sag in P079 UBCs is consistent with previous work showing that OFF UBCs have a larger h-current than ON UBCs.
source: This is consistent with previous work showing that OFF UBCs have a larger h-current than ON UBCs (Kim et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Crossing the GRP-Cre/Ai9 mice with the P079 mice resulted in triple transgenic mice that expressed tdTomato and mCitrine in almost entirely separate subpopulations of UBCs—only 3 out of 944 UBCs that were labeled expressed both fluorescent proteins.
source: Crossing the GRP-Cre/Ai9 mice with the P079 mice resulted in triple transgenic mice that expressed tdTomato and mCitrine in almost entirely separate subpopulations of UBCs—only 3 out of 944 UBCs that were labeled expressed both fluorescent proteins.
evidence: This claim is supported by counting labeled cells in the triple transgenic mice.

claim: GRP and P079 UBCs were present in the lobes of the cerebellar vermis in different densities.
source: GRP and P079 UBCs were present in the lobes of the cerebellar vermis in different densities (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: More GRP UBCs than P079 UBCs were present in lobes VI–IX.
source: More GRP UBCs than P079 UBCs were present in lobes VI–IX, with few of either subtype in lobes II–V.
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging and counting data.

claim: The highest density of both UBC subtypes was in lobe X.
source: The highest density of both UBC subtypes was in lobe X, which is where we focused the following analyses (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The cross-sectional area of GRP UBCs was significantly smaller than that of P079 UBCs.
source: We found that the cross-sectional area of GRP UBCs was significantly smaller than that of P079 UBCs (GRP: 68.75 ± 9.69 µm2, mean ± SD, n = 92; P079: 74.47 ± 12.53 µm2, mean ± SD, n = 114, t-test, p=0.0004)
evidence: This claim is supported by morphological measurements.

claim: The smaller soma size of GRP UBCs is consistent with the electrophysiological analysis of their membrane capacitance.
source: which is consistent with our electrophysiological analysis of their membrane capacitance (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is an inference connecting morphological and electrophysiological data.

claim: The distribution of GRP and P079 UBCs supports their identity as ON and OFF UBCs as the density of mGluR1(+) ON UBCs is higher in the ventral leaflet of lobe X and the density of calretinin(+) OFF UBCs is higher in the dorsal leaflet.
source: The distribution of GRP and P079 UBCs also supports their identity as ON and OFF UBCs as the density of mGluR1(+) ON UBCs is higher in the ventral leaflet of lobe X and the density of calretinin(+) OFF UBCs is higher in the dorsal leaflet (Nunzi et al., 2002; Sekerková et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by the distribution data and citations to prior work.

claim: 98.1% (155/158) of the GRP/Ai9 UBCs expressed mGluR1 in their dendritic brushes.
source: We found that 98.1% (155/158) of the GRP/Ai9 UBCs expressed mGluR1 in their dendritic brushes (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: The GRP/Ai9/mGluR1(+) population represented 20.9% (155/741) of the total population of mGluR1(+) UBCs.
source: The GRP/Ai9/mGluR1(+) population represented 20.9% (155/741) of the total population of mGluR1(+) UBCs.
evidence: This claim is supported by counting immunolabeled cells.

claim: 0/149 GRP/Ai9 UBCs expressed calretinin.
source: 0/149 GRP/Ai9 UBCs expressed calretinin in a separate series of slices (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 3C and D.

claim: The GRP line labels about 1/5th of the ON UBCs and does not label OFF UBCs.
source: Thus, the GRP line labels about 1/5th of the ON UBCs and does not label OFF UBCs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the immunohistochemical data.

claim: 92.2% (284/308) of the P079 UBCs were calretinin(+).
source: Using the same triple transgenic mice and immunohistochemical approach described above, 92.2% (284/308) of the P079 UBCs were calretinin(+) (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 3C and D.

claim: The P079 UBCs represent 70.5% (284/403) of the total calretinin(+) population.
source: The P079 UBCs represent 70.5% (284/403) of the total calretinin(+) population.
evidence: This claim is supported by counting immunolabeled cells.

claim: 61.3% (200/326) of the P079 UBCs appeared mGluR1(+).
source: We were surprised to find, however, that 61.3% (200/326) of the P079 UBCs appeared mGluR1(+).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemical data.

claim: The P079/mGluR1(+) UBCs represent 27.0% (200/741) of the total mGluR1(+) population.
source: This represents 27.0% (200/741) of the total mGluR1(+) population.
evidence: This claim is supported by counting immunolabeled cells.

claim: The P079/mGluR1(+) UBCs could be differentiated from P079/mGluR1(-) UBCs by their lower expression of mCitrine.
source: These P079/mGluR1(+) UBCs could be differentiated from P079/mGluR1(-) UBCs by their lower expression of mCitrine: the relative labeling intensity of the mGluR1(+) P079 UBCs, after amplification with an anti-GFP antibody, was less than half of the more common mGluR1(-) P079 UBCs (43.2% soma pixel intensity relative to mGluR1(-) P079 UBCs, n = 34 z-planes with at least one of each subtype, t-test, p=8.403e-6).
evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence intensity measurements.

claim: The cross-sectional area of the mGluR1(+) P079 somas was significantly smaller than the mGluR1(-) P079 somas.
source: In addition, the cross-sectional area of the mGluR1(+) P079 somas was 60.62 ± 13.67 µm2, mean ± SD, n = 52 and significantly smaller than the mGluR1(-) P079 somas (72.48 ± 16.90 µm2 mean ± SD, n = 40, t-test, p=0.00035).
evidence: This claim is supported by morphological measurements.

claim: It is likely that the P079 UBCs that express a low density of mCitrine were not able to be visualized in electrophysiological experiments because their native fluorescence was below the level of detection.
source: It is likely that the P079 UBCs that express a low density of mCitrine were not able to be visualized in our electrophysiological experiments because their native fluorescence was below the level of detection.
evidence: This is an inference based on the fluorescence intensity data.

claim: The observation that some mGluR1(+) UBCs are labeled in the P079 mouse line precludes its use for expressing genes in OFF UBCs specifically.
source: Unfortunately, the observation that some mGluR1(+) UBCs are labeled in the P079 mouse line precludes its use for expressing genes in OFF UBCs specifically.
evidence: This is an inference based on the immunohistochemical data.

claim: 97.8% (132/135) of the GRP/Ai9 UBCs in the dorsal cochlear nucleus expressed mGluR1 in their dendritic brushes.
source: We found that 97.8% (132/135) of the GRP/Ai9 UBCs expressed mGluR1 in their dendritic brushes (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: The GRP/Ai9/mGluR1(+) population in the dorsal cochlear nucleus represented 34.2% (132/386) of the population of mGluR1(+) UBCs.
source: The GRP/Ai9/mGluR1(+) population represented 34.2% (132/386) of the population of mGluR1(+) UBCs and is therefore a subpopulation of about 1/3 of the mGluR1(+) ON UBCs.
evidence: This claim is supported by counting immunolabeled cells in the dorsal cochlear nucleus.

claim: 0/115 GRP/Ai9 UBCs in the dorsal cochlear nucleus expressed calretinin.
source: In a separate series of slices, 0/115 GRP/Ai9 UBCs expressed calretinin and is therefore useful for expressing genes in a subset of ON UBCs without expression in OFF UBCs in the dorsal cochlear nucleus.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemical data.

claim: The GRP line is useful for expressing genes in a subset of ON UBCs without expression in OFF UBCs in the dorsal cochlear nucleus.
source: In a separate series of slices, 0/115 GRP/Ai9 UBCs expressed calretinin and is therefore useful for expressing genes in a subset of ON UBCs without expression in OFF UBCs in the dorsal cochlear nucleus.
evidence: This is an inference based on the immunohistochemical data.

claim: 89.7% (140/156) of the P079 UBCs in the dorsal cochlear nucleus were calretinin(+).
source: We also found that 89.7% (140/156) of the P079 UBCs were calretinin(+) (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 4C and D.

claim: The P079 UBCs in the dorsal cochlear nucleus represent 85.9% (140/163) of the total calretinin(+) population.
source: The P079 UBCs represent 85.9% (140/163) of the total calretinin(+) population.
evidence: This claim is supported by counting immunolabeled cells in the dorsal cochlear nucleus.

claim: 56.7% (127/224) of the P079 UBCs in the dorsal cochlear nucleus were mGluR1(+).
source: Similar to our results in the cerebellum, we found that 56.7% (127/224) of the P079 UBCs were mGluR1(+).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemical data.

claim: The P079/mGluR1(+) UBCs in the dorsal cochlear nucleus represent 32.9% (127/386) of the mGluR1(+) population.
source: This represents 32.9% (127/386) of the mGluR1(+) population.
evidence: This claim is supported by counting immunolabeled cells in the dorsal cochlear nucleus.

claim: The P079/mGluR1(+) UBCs in the dorsal cochlear nucleus were identifiable by their significantly lower intensity of mCitrine after antibody amplification.
source: As in the cerebellum, these P079/mGluR1(+) UBCs were identifiable by their significantly lower intensity of mCitrine after antibody amplification (43.5% intensity compared to mGluR1(-) P079 UBCs, n = 19 z-planes with at least one of each type, t-test, p=1.352e-6).
evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence intensity measurements.

claim: The expression pattern in the dorsal cochlear nucleus of UBCs in the GRP and P079 mouse lines mirrors that of the cerebellum.
source: Thus, the expression pattern in the dorsal cochlear nucleus of UBCs in these two mouse lines mirrors that of the cerebellum.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparing the data from cerebellum and dorsal cochlear nucleus.

claim: GRP ON UBCs provide synaptic input to P079 OFF UBCs.
source: Several examples of such synaptic connections were identified, indicating that GRP ON UBCs provide synaptic input to P079 OFF UBCs (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by anatomical data shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: OFF UBCs provide synaptic input to ON UBCs.
source: Using the same approach, we found OFF UBC axon terminals (P079 and calretinin(+)) contacting ON UBC brushes (GRP) (Figure 5C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by anatomical data shown in Figure 5C and D.

claim: UBC subtypes synapse on one another and may introduce complex spiking patterns.
source: However, these results do reveal that UBC subtypes synapse on one another and may introduce complex spiking patterns.
evidence: This is an inference based on the anatomical data and speculation about function.

claim: GRP ON UBCs target mGluR1(+) UBCs that are not transgenicially labeled in the GRP mouse line.
source: These examples show that GRP ON UBCs target mGluR1(+) UBCs that are not transgenicially labeled in the GRP mouse line.
evidence: This claim is supported by anatomical data shown in Figure 6.

claim: GRP ON UBCs project to other GRP ON UBCs in a feed-forward excitatory circuit that is likely to prolong the duration of an excitatory signal.
source: Thus, GRP ON UBCs project to other GRP ON UBCs in a feed-forward excitatory circuit that is likely to prolong the duration of an excitatory signal.
evidence: This is an inference based on the anatomical data shown in Figure 7 and speculation about function.

claim: OFF UBCs project axons to other OFF UBCs.
source: Several examples for OFF to OFF UBC synaptic connections were confirmed anatomically (Figure 8).
evidence: This claim is supported by anatomical data shown in Figure 8.

claim: Calretinin(+) OFF UBCs provide input to one another.
source: Several examples are shown, confirming that calretinin(+) OFF UBCs provide input to one another (Figure 9B–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by anatomical data shown in Figure 9B-D.

claim: An axon terminal appeared to contact the soma of a postsynaptic UBC, which has been previously reported to occur between extrinsic mossy fibers and UBC somata.
source: In one of these examples, an axon terminal appeared to contact the soma of a postsynaptic UBC (Figure 9C), which has been previously reported to occur between extrinsic mossy fibers and UBC somata (Balmer and Trussell, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by anatomical data shown in Figure 9C and a citation to prior work.

claim: The presence of large or small contacts implies differences in synaptic strength, suggesting that OFF UBCs may provide strong synaptic signals to one another or presumably weaker signals that are subsequently integrated with other inputs.
source: The presence of large or small contacts implies differences in synaptic strength, suggesting that OFF UBCs may provide strong synaptic signals to one another (Figure 9B) or presumably weaker signals (Figure 9C and D) that are subsequently integrated with other inputs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the anatomical data shown in Figure 9 and speculation about synaptic strength.

claim: Presynaptic input to an ON UBC produced bursts of action potentials that multiplied in duration in a circuit with an intermediate ON UBC.
source: Presynaptic input to an ON UBC produced bursts of action potentials that multiplied in duration in a circuit with an intermediate ON UBC (Figure 10A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling data shown in Figure 10A-C.

claim: Three presynaptic spikes in a burst lasting 19.6 ms produced a burst of 12 action potentials in the first UBC, lasting 358.0 ms, and 35 action potentials in the second UBC, lasting 1175.3 ms, ~60 times longer than the initial presynaptic input.
source: Three presynaptic spikes in a burst lasting 19.6 ms produced a burst of 12 action potentials in the first UBC, lasting 358.0 ms, and 35 action potentials in the second UBC, lasting 1175.3 ms, ~60 times longer than the initial presynaptic input (Figure 10A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling data shown in Figure 10A and B.

claim: The enhancement of the spiking duration both in the first and second ON UBC was more pronounced with shorter bursts of presynaptic input and began to plateau at longer durations of input.
source: The enhancement of the spiking duration both in the first and second ON UBC was more pronounced with shorter bursts of presynaptic input and began to plateau at longer durations of input (Figure 10C).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling data shown in Figure 10C.

claim: The plateau in spiking duration occurs because the rebound AMPA receptor-mediated slow EPSC that occurs at the end of synaptic stimulation in ON UBCs reaches a maximum after ~100 ms of synaptic stimulation.
source: The plateau in spiking duration occurs because the rebound AMPA receptor-mediated slow EPSC that occurs at the end of synaptic stimulation in ON UBCs reaches a maximum after ~100 ms of synaptic stimulation (Lu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an inference based on the modeling results and a citation to prior work.

claim: When an intermediate ON UBC was present between the presynaptic axon and the OFF UBC, the synaptic signal to the OFF UBC was extended, and therefore increased the mGluR2 current, markedly lengthening the duration of the pause in spiking.
source: When an intermediate ON UBC was present between the presynaptic axon and the OFF UBC, the synaptic signal to the OFF UBC was extended, and therefore increased the mGluR2 current, markedly lengthening the duration of the pause in spiking (Figure 10E and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling data shown in Figure 10E and F.

claim: The presence of an intermediate ON UBC increased the duration of the pause in the postsynaptic OFF UBC by ~940 ms following 1–10 presynaptic action potentials.
source: Indeed, the presence of an intermediate ON UBC increased the duration of the pause in the postsynaptic OFF UBC by ~940 ms following 1–10 presynaptic action potentials (indicated by an upward shift in the curve in Figure 10G).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling data shown in Figure 10G.

claim: Presynaptic input to the intermediate OFF UBC paused both its firing and its release of glutamate onto the postsynaptic ON UBC, which therefore produced a pause in the postsynaptic ON UBC.
source: Presynaptic input to the intermediate OFF UBC paused both its firing and its release of glutamate onto the postsynaptic ON UBC, which therefore produced a pause in the postsynaptic ON UBC.
evidence: This is an inference based on the computational modeling results.

claim: The pause in the postsynaptic ON UBC only occurred after a delay of about 370 ms due to the slow AMPA receptor-mediated EPSC in the ON UBC that decayed slowly until it no longer drove spiking.
source: However, this pause only occurred after a delay of about 370 ms due to the slow AMPA receptor-mediated EPSC in the ON UBC that decayed slowly until it no longer drove spiking.
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling data.

claim: An intermediate OFF UBC converts the usual excitatory ON UBC response to a pause that is similar to that of the OFF UBC itself.
source: Thus, an intermediate OFF UBC converts the usual excitatory ON UBC response to a pause that is similar to that of the OFF UBC itself.
evidence: This is an inference based on the computational modeling results.

claim: In a circuit with a spontaneously firing OFF UBC synapsing onto another OFF UBC, the tonic glutamatergic input and mGluR2 inhibition prevented spontaneous spiking in the postsynaptic cell.
source: In a circuit with a spontaneously firing OFF UBC synapsing onto another OFF UBC (labeled OFF1 and OFF2, respectively, in Figure 11C and D), the tonic glutamatergic input and mGluR2 inhibition prevented spontaneous spiking in the postsynaptic cell.
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling data shown in Figure 11C and D.

claim: When the intermediate OFF UBC received a burst of presynaptic input, it was inhibited by its own mGluR2 current and therefore stopped firing, thereby disinhibiting the postsynaptic OFF UBC, which then fired after a delay.
source: When the intermediate OFF UBC received a burst of presynaptic input, it was inhibited by its own mGluR2 current and therefore stopped firing, thereby disinhibiting the postsynaptic OFF UBC, which then fired after a delay (Figure 11C).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling data shown in Figure 11C.

claim: The duration of the delayed firing in the second postsynaptic OFF UBC depended on the duration of presynaptic input signal to the intermediate UBC.
source: The duration of the delayed firing in the second postsynaptic OFF UBC depended on the duration of presynaptic input signal to the intermediate UBC (Figure 11D).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling data shown in Figure 11D.

claim: The delay between the last spike in the intermediate OFF UBC and the first spike in the postsynaptic OFF UBC was contingent on the slow decay of the mGluR2 current and was 1082.7 ms in the example.
source: Moreover, the delay between the last spike in the intermediate OFF UBC and the first spike in the postsynaptic OFF UBC was contingent on the slow decay of the mGluR2 current and was 1082.7 ms in the example in Figure 11C.
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling data shown in Figure 11C.

claim: Feed-forward circuits of ON and OFF UBCs transform presynaptic signals by producing an extended spike burst (ON to ON), extended pause (ON to OFF), pause after a delay (OFF to ON), or burst after a delay (OFF to OFF).
source: In summary, our modeling suggests that feed-forward circuits of ON and OFF UBCs transform presynaptic signals by producing an extended spike burst (ON to ON), extended pause (ON to OFF), pause after a delay (OFF to ON), or burst after a delay (OFF to OFF) (Figure 12).
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the computational modeling results shown in Figure 12.

claim: This diversification of spiking patterns and durations may be important for maintaining sensory representations of movement and mechanisms of adaptive learning.
source: This diversification of spiking patterns and durations may be important for maintaining sensory representations of movement and mechanisms of adaptive learning.
evidence: This is speculation about the functional significance of the modeling results.

claim: Virtually no neurons expressed both fluorescent proteins in the GRP-Cre/Ai9 and P079 crossed mice.
source: Virtually no neurons expressed both fluorescent proteins.
evidence: This claim is supported by the observation that only 3 out of 944 UBCs expressed both fluorescent proteins.

claim: All GRP UBCs expressed mGluR1 and most P079 UBCs expressed calretinin in both cerebellum and dorsal cochlear nucleus.
source: Immunohistochemical analysis showed that all GRP UBCs expressed mGluR1 and most P079 UBCs expressed calretinin in both cerebellum and dorsal cochlear nucleus.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemical data.

claim: GRP and P079 UBCs had different average soma sizes and distributions in the cerebellum.
source: GRP and P079 UBCs had different average soma sizes and distributions in the cerebellum.
evidence: This claim is supported by morphological measurements and imaging data.

claim: The membrane capacitance and excitability of GRP and P079 UBCs were so distinct that the distributions of these properties were almost nonoverlapping.
source: Their membrane capacitance and excitability were so distinct that the distributions of these properties were almost nonoverlapping.
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data.

claim: Some UBC subtypes are genetically and functionally distinct, despite the observation that when the entire population of UBCs is examined, their electrophysiological responses form a continuum from entirely excited by glutamate to entirely inhibited by glutamate.
source: These results provide further evidence that some UBC subtypes are genetically and functionally distinct, despite the observation that when the entire population of UBCs is examined, their electrophysiological responses form a continuum from entirely excited by glutamate to entirely inhibited by glutamate (Guo et al., 2021; Kozareva et al., 2021).
evidence: This is an inference based on the current data and citations to prior work.

claim: Axon terminals from one UBC subtype contact the dendritic brushes of the other UBC subtype.
source: The UBCs in these mouse lines expressed the fluorescent proteins throughout their axons and presynaptic terminals, which revealed for the first time that axon terminals from one UBC subtype contact the dendric brushes of the other UBC subtype.
evidence: This claim is supported by anatomical data.

claim: UBCs of the same subtype provide input to one another.
source: We also showed that UBCs of the same subtype provide input to one another by labeling GRP or calretinin-Cre UBCs with different fluorescent proteins using the Brainbow2.1-Confetti reporter line.
evidence: This claim is supported by anatomical data using the Brainbow approach.

claim: Earlier work reported that mGluR1(+) UBCs and calretinin(+) UBCs form parallel pathways.
source: Earlier work reported that mGluR1(+) UBCs and calretinin(+) UBCs form parallel pathways (Nunzi et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The current data extends the previous result by showing that the even more specific subtypes of GRP or P079 UBCs provide input to members of their own subtype.
source: Our current data extends the previous result by showing that the even more specific subtypes of GRP or P079 UBCs provide input to members of their own subtype.
evidence: This is an inference based on the current anatomical data and comparison to prior work.

claim: Networks of UBCs could provide the granule layer with a circuit mechanism to diversify and extend the pattern of spiking produced by mossy fiber input.
source: These networks of UBCs could provide the granule layer with a circuit mechanism to diversify and extend the pattern of spiking produced by mossy fiber input.
evidence: This is speculation about the functional significance of the anatomical findings.

claim: Anatomically identifiable connections between UBCs were not present in all brain slices and finding them required a careful search.
source: Anatomically identifiable connections between UBCs were not present in all brain slices and finding them required a careful search.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental observations.

claim: UBC labeling was sparse due to the highly specific genetic labeling techniques and further sparsification by the Brainbow reporter, which made it impossible to accurately estimate the density of these UBC to UBC connections.
source: UBC labeling was sparse due to the highly specific genetic labeling techniques and further sparsification by the Brainbow reporter, which made it impossible to accurately estimate the density of these UBC to UBC connections.
evidence: This is an explanation of a limitation of the experimental approach.

claim: Electrophysiological evidence suggests that UBC to UBC connections are not common because spontaneous EPSCs that would indicate a spontaneously firing presynaptic UBC are not frequently observed in intracellular recordings of UBCs in acute brain slices.
source: Electrophysiological evidence suggests that UBC to UBC connections are not common because spontaneous EPSCs that would indicate a spontaneously firing presynaptic UBC are not frequently observed in intracellular recordings of UBCs in acute brain slices.
evidence: This is an inference based on electrophysiological observations.

claim: Only 4 out of 140 UBCs were reported to have indirect evidence of a firing presynaptic UBC, which suggests that UBC to UBC connections may be rare.
source: In an analysis of feed-forward excitation of granule layer neurons, only 4 out of 140 UBCs were reported to have this indirect evidence of a firing presynaptic UBC (van Dorp and De Zeeuw, 2015), which suggests that UBC to UBC connections may be rare.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work and inference about connection density.

claim: Previous work using organotypic slice cultures from P8 mice estimated that 2/3 of the UBC population receives input from other UBCs.
source: On the other hand, previous work using organotypic slice cultures from P8 mice estimated that 2/3 of the UBC population receives input from other UBCs (Nunzi and Mugnaini, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The higher density of UBC to UBC connections in organotypic cultures could be due to the young age of the brains used, which is before UBCs have matured, and also due to increased collateral sprouting that can occur in culture.
source: This suggests a much higher density of UBC to UBC connections, but could be due to the young age of the brains used, which is before UBCs have matured (Morin et al., 2001), and also due to increased collateral sprouting that can occur in culture (Jaeger et al., 1988).
evidence: This is speculation about the reasons for differences between studies, supported by citations.

claim: A study that imaged 2–4-week-old rat cerebellar slices at an electron microscopic level found that 4 out of 14 UBC axon terminals contacted UBC brushes.
source: Another study imaged 2–4-week-old rat cerebellar slices at an electron microscopic level and found that 4 out of 14 UBC axon terminals contacted UBC brushes (Diño et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The final output and main target of UBCs are granule cells.
source: However, it is important to emphasize that the final output and main target of UBCs are granule cells.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: Most of the labeled UBC axon terminals did not synapse on UBCs and are therefore presumed to synapse on numerous granule cells.
source: Most of the labeled UBC axon terminals did not synapse on UBCs and are therefore presumed to synapse on numerous granule cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the anatomical observations.

claim: Even the axon terminals that targeted UBCs likely also contacted granule cells.
source: Even the axon terminals that targeted UBCs likely also contacted granule cells.
evidence: This is speculation based on the known anatomy of UBC axon terminals.

claim: UBCs are interneurons that, when positioned between mossy fibers and granule cells, modify the input to granule cells and have the capacity to synchronize the firing of large ensembles of granule cells via their branching axons and large terminals.
source: Thus, UBCs are interneurons that, when positioned between mossy fibers and granule cells, modify the input to granule cells and have the capacity to synchronize the firing of large ensembles of granule cells via their branching axons and large terminals.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known properties of UBCs.

claim: If present, three or more UBCs in series could extend and transform the input in even more dramatic ways.
source: If present, three or more UBCs in series could extend and transform the input in even more dramatic ways.
evidence: This is speculation about potential circuits not directly observed.

claim: The temporal diversity that UBC circuits generate may underlie the flexibility of the cerebellum to coordinate movements over a broad range of behaviors.
source: The temporal diversity that UBC circuits generate may underlie the flexibility of the cerebellum to coordinate movements over a broad range of behaviors.
evidence: This is speculation about the functional significance of UBC circuits.

claim: The model does not consider feed-forward and lateral inhibition from Golgi cells, which shapes the spiking of UBCs in response to afferent stimulation.
source: One limitation of the model is that it does not consider feed-forward and lateral inhibition from Golgi cells, which shapes the spiking of UBCs in response to afferent stimulation.
evidence: This is a description of a limitation of the computational model.

claim: Golgi cells receive mossy fiber input and inhibit UBCs through their corelease of GABA and glycine.
source: Golgi cells receive mossy fiber input and inhibit UBCs through their corelease of GABA and glycine (Dugué et al., 2005; Rousseau et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Golgi cells control the temporal dynamics of the firing of granule cells as well as their gain and are critical to larger-scale dynamics of the cerebellar cortical network.
source: Golgi cells control the temporal dynamics of the firing of granule cells as well as their gain (Rossi et al., 2003; Kanichay and Silver, 2008) and are critical to larger-scale dynamics of the cerebellar cortical network (D'Angelo, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Purkinje cells provide additional inhibition to ON UBCs that could influence how UBC circuits transform signals.
source: Purkinje cells provide additional inhibition to ON UBCs that could influence how UBC circuits transform signals (Guo et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Vestibular afferents that encode head movements synapse on both UBCs and granule cells.
source: Vestibular afferents that encode head movements synapse on both UBCs and granule cells.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: Granule cells that receive vestibular input are likely to fire in phase with the input signal.
source: Granule cells that receive this input are likely to fire in phase with the input signal.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known properties of granule cells.

claim: A single intermediate UBC would shift the phase of firing of its postsynaptic granule cells, depending on the UBC's response to glutamatergic input.
source: A single intermediate UBC would shift the phase of firing of its postsynaptic granule cells, depending on the UBC's response to glutamatergic input, which varies from nearly complete inhibition (e.g., P079 OFF UBC) to complete excitation (e.g., GRP ON UBC) (Guo et al., 2021; Kozareva et al., 2021).
evidence: This is an inference based on the modeling results and citations to prior work.

claim: An intermediate ON UBC between a presynaptic input and another UBC extended the signal markedly in the models.
source: For example, an intermediate ON UBC between a presynaptic input and another UBC extended the signal markedly in our models.
evidence: This claim is supported by the computational modeling results.

claim: In circuits with an intermediate OFF UBC, the postsynaptic UBC's signal was inverted: ON UBCs paused when they were no longer driven by glutamate, and OFF UBCs fired when they were no longer inhibited by glutamate.
source: In circuits with an intermediate OFF UBC, the postsynaptic UBCs signal was inverted: ON UBCs paused when they were no longer driven by glutamate, and OFF UBCs fired when they were no longer inhibited by glutamate.
evidence: This claim is supported by the computational modeling results.

claim: The signal that granule cells subsequently receive would be a burst or pause in firing that lasts for hundreds or thousands of milliseconds.
source: The signal that granule cells subsequently receive would be a burst or pause in firing that lasts for hundreds or thousands of milliseconds.
evidence: This is an inference based on the modeling results.

claim: These transformations could provide a circuit mechanism for maintaining a sensory representation of movement for seconds, which is thought to be necessary to modulate low-frequency vestibular responses such as compensatory eye movements.
source: We suggest that these transformations could provide a circuit mechanism for maintaining a sensory representation of movement for seconds, which is thought to be necessary to modulate low-frequency vestibular responses such as compensatory eye movements.
evidence: This is speculation about the functional significance of the modeling results.

claim: The delays introduced by an intermediate UBC were due to the slow decay of the excitatory or inhibitory synaptic currents produced by the presynaptic input.
source: The delays introduced by an intermediate UBC were due to the slow decay of the excitatory or inhibitory synaptic currents produced by the presynaptic input.
evidence: This is an inference based on the modeling results.

claim: Other cellular and synaptic properties that would shape the timing of pauses, delays, and bursts include the amount of glutamate released and the rate of its removal, the geometry of the extracellular space, glutamate receptor number and localization, short-term synaptic plasticity, currents underlying rebound spiking, and intrinsic excitability.
source: Other cellular and synaptic properties that would shape the timing of pauses, delays, and bursts include the amount of glutamate released and the rate of its removal, the geometry of the extracellular space, glutamate receptor number and localization, short-term synaptic plasticity, currents underlying rebound spiking, and intrinsic excitability (Kim et al., 2012; Kinney et al., 2013; Locatelli et al., 2013; Zampini et al., 2016; Lu et al., 2017; Balmer et al., 2021a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The combination of numerous mechanisms that shape the signal as it is transmitted along the granule layer circuit could produce tunable delay lines essential for sensory representation on an enormous range of time scales.
source: The combination of numerous mechanisms that shape the signal as it is transmitted along the granule layer circuit could produce tunable delay lines essential for sensory representation on an enormous range of time scales.
evidence: This is speculation about the functional significance of the various mechanisms.

claim: Extending the duration of a sensory feedback signal may also be essential for motor learning when there is a significant delay between the motor output and the sensory feedback.
source: Extending the duration of a sensory feedback signal may also be essential for motor learning when there is a significant delay between the motor output and the sensory feedback, for example, when throwing an object at distant target, a challenge referred to as the credit assignment problem (Sutton and Barto, 1981; Raymond and Lisberger, 1998; Suvrathan, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on motor learning.

claim: There are a variety of ways that the cerebellum could extend a signal in time, such as slow axonal conduction, long membrane time constants, inhibition followed by rebound spiking, and slow intracellular processes.
source: There are a variety of ways that the cerebellum could extend a signal in time, such as slow axonal conduction, long membrane time constants, inhibition followed by rebound spiking, and slow intracellular processes (Braitenberg, 1967; Rossi et al., 1995; Fiala et al., 1996; Hooper et al., 2002; D'Angelo and De Zeeuw, 2009; van Dorp and De Zeeuw, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: UBC circuits represent another mechanism that could prolong granule cell firing and contribute to the maintenance of sensory signals that underlie motor learning in behaviors with delayed sensory feedback.
source: UBCs circuits represent another mechanism that could prolong granule cell firing and contribute to the maintenance of sensory signals that underlie motor learning in behaviors with delayed sensory feedback.
evidence: This is speculation about the functional significance of UBC circuits.

claim: The diversification of spiking patterns by intermediate UBCs may contribute to the pattern separation that is necessary for theories of cerebellar learning.
source: The diversification of spiking patterns by intermediate UBCs may contribute to the pattern separation that is necessary for theories of cerebellar learning (Marr, 1969; Albus, 1971; Ito, 1982; Kennedy et al., 2014; Zampini et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on cerebellar learning theories and speculation.

claim: In the electrosensory lobe of electric fish, UBCs are essential to produce temporally diverse and delayed spiking patterns that are necessary for accurate cancellation of self-generated signals.
source: In one of the best understood cerebellum-like circuits, the electrosensory lobe of electric fish, UBCs are essential to produce temporally diverse and delayed spiking patterns that are necessary for accurate cancellation of self-generated signals (Kennedy et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: A post-inhibitory rebound that occurred in UBCs may account for the delayed spiking patterns in the electrosensory lobe.
source: The authors report that a post-inhibitory rebound that occurred in UBCs may account for the delayed spiking patterns.
evidence: This claim is based on a citation to prior work.

claim: The presence of synaptic pathways with multiple UBCs could contribute to long pauses and delays that may be critical for adaptive learning on time scales ranging from hundreds of milliseconds to tens of seconds.
source: The presence of synaptic pathways with multiple UBCs could contribute to these long pauses and delays that may be critical for adaptive learning on time scales ranging from hundreds of milliseconds to tens of seconds.
evidence: This is speculation about the functional significance of UBC circuits.

claim: The firing rates of putative UBCs recorded in vivo in the vestibular cerebellum of mammals follow head velocity and eye movements, in some cases with delays of hundreds of milliseconds.
source: The firing rates of putative UBCs recorded in vivo in the vestibular cerebellum of mammals follow head velocity and eye movements, in some cases with delays of hundreds of milliseconds (Simpson et al., 2005; Barmack and Yakhnitsa, 2008; Hensbroek et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The long delays observed in vivo could be implemented by feed-forward circuits containing multiple UBCs.
source: Our data suggests that these long delays could be implemented by feed-forward circuits containing multiple UBCs.
evidence: This is speculation based on the current findings.

claim: In lobe X, ON UBCs defined by their electrophysiological response or mGluR1-expression receive input from both primary vestibular afferents and second-order mossy fibers from the vestibular nucleus, while OFF UBCs only receive vestibular nuclear input.
source: In lobe X, ON UBCs defined by their electrophysiological response or mGluR1-expression receive input from both primary vestibular afferents and second-order mossy fibers from the vestibular nucleus, while OFF UBCs only receive vestibular nuclear input (Balmer and Trussell, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.
